title: Schema design and relations
intro: A good database schema makes valid data easy to store and invalid data difficult to create. In this lesson, you will design the database for a small booking app and learn how keys, relationships and database constraints protect the data your application depends on.
body:
## Start with the domain

Before creating tables, describe what the application actually needs to store.

Imagine a small booking application for a hair salon, consultant or fitness studio. Customers book services such as a haircut, consultation or training session.

We need to represent three main things:

- a **customer** who makes bookings
- a **service** that can be booked
- a **booking** connecting a customer with a service at a particular time

This gives us three tables:

~~~text
customers
services
bookings
~~~

The important database design question is not simply "What tables should I create?" It is:

**What facts exist in the domain, and how are those facts related?**

Once that is clear, the table structure becomes much easier to design.

## An ER diagram in plain text

An **ER diagram (Entity-Relationship diagram)** describes entities and their relationships. We can represent the booking application with ASCII:

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "The booking schema as an ER diagram", "nodes": [{"id": "u", "label": "users", "sub": "id · email UNIQUE", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "b", "label": "bookings", "sub": "user_id · room_id · starts_at", "kind": "db", "highlight": true}, {"id": "r", "label": "rooms", "sub": "id · name · capacity CHECK > 0", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "rt", "label": "room_tags", "sub": "room_id · tag_id", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "t", "label": "tags", "sub": "id · name", "kind": "db"}], "edges": [{"from": "u", "to": "b", "label": "1 : N"}, {"from": "r", "to": "b", "label": "1 : N"}, {"from": "r", "to": "rt", "label": "1 : N"}, {"from": "t", "to": "rt", "label": "1 : N"}]}
~~~

~~~text
+------------------+       +------------------+
|    customers     |       |     services     |
+------------------+       +------------------+
| id PK            |       | id PK            |
| name             |       | name             |
| email            |       | duration_minutes |
+------------------+       +------------------+
        | 1                         | 1
        |                           |
        |                           |
        | many                      | many
        v                           v
              +------------------+
              |     bookings     |
              +------------------+
              | id PK            |
              | customer_id FK   |
              | service_id FK    |
              | starts_at        |
              | status           |
              +------------------+
~~~

`PK` means **primary key**. `FK` means **foreign key**.

Each booking belongs to one customer and one service. A customer can have many bookings, and a service can appear in many bookings.

This is a pair of one-to-many relationships.

## Primary keys

A **primary key** uniquely identifies a row in a table.

For example:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL
);
~~~

Two customers can have the same name, but they cannot have the same primary key.

The primary key gives application code a stable way to refer to a particular row.

For example:

~~~text
/api/customers/42
~~~

can identify customer 42 regardless of whether the customer's name later changes.

### Generated IDs in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL supports identity columns for generated numeric IDs. In the production database, we can use:

~~~sql
id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
~~~

The database generates the value when a row is inserted.

You may also encounter older PostgreSQL schemas using `SERIAL`. `SERIAL` is an older convenience mechanism based on sequences. For new PostgreSQL schemas, identity columns are generally the clearer modern choice.

Our browser exercise uses SQLite-compatible syntax instead:

~~~sql
id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
~~~

The exercise is about the schema relationships and constraints, not PostgreSQL-specific ID syntax.

## Natural keys vs generated keys

A **natural key** is a value that already exists in the domain and uniquely identifies something.

An email address might appear to be a natural key for a customer. However, email addresses can change, and some domains may have unusual rules around uniqueness.

A generated ID is often a simpler primary key:

~~~text
customers
id: 42
email: anna@example.com
~~~

The ID identifies the row while the email can have a separate `UNIQUE` constraint.

This gives us a useful separation:

- primary key: stable database identity
- unique constraint: a business/data rule about a value

## One-to-many relationships

A one-to-many relationship means one row in table A can be related to many rows in table B.

For example:

~~~text
one customer
     |
     +---- booking
     +---- booking
     +---- booking
~~~

The foreign key goes on the many side:

~~~sql
customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES customers(id)
~~~

The `bookings.customer_id` column points to `customers.id`.

This means the database can check that a booking refers to an existing customer.

The same principle applies to services:

~~~sql
service_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES services(id)
~~~

A service can therefore be referenced by many bookings.

## Many-to-many relationships

Sometimes two entities can each have many relationships to the other.

~~~callout tip Many-to-many needs a table in the middle
A room has many tags and a tag belongs to many rooms. Neither table can hold the list, so create `room_tags(room_id, tag_id)` with a composite primary key — each row is one link.
~~~

Imagine a task manager where tasks can have many labels and each label can belong to many tasks.

You cannot represent that cleanly with one `label_id` column in `tasks` because a task may have several labels.

Instead, create a **join table**:

~~~text
tasks
  |
  | many
  v
 task_labels
  ^
  | many
  |
labels
~~~

The table might look like:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE task_labels (
    task_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tasks(id),
    label_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES labels(id),
    PRIMARY KEY (task_id, label_id)
);
~~~

Each row represents one relationship.

For example:

~~~text
task_id | label_id
--------+---------
1       | 2
1       | 5
3       | 2
~~~

Task 1 has labels 2 and 5, while task 3 has label 2.

In the booking application, customers and services do not need a many-to-many join table because the booking itself is the relationship. A booking records which customer chose which service and when.

## NOT NULL

`NOT NULL` says that a column must contain a value.

~~~sql
name TEXT NOT NULL
~~~

A customer without a name is not valid in our model, so the database should reject such a row.

This is important because application code is not the only thing that can interact with a database. Another script, migration, admin tool or future service could accidentally insert invalid data.

Database constraints provide a final line of defence for data integrity.

## UNIQUE

`UNIQUE` prevents duplicate values.

~~~sql
email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
~~~

This says that every customer must have an email and that no two customers can have the same email.

You should not rely only on code such as:

~~~text
if email does not exist:
    create customer
~~~

Two requests can arrive at nearly the same time. Both could check before either has inserted the row.

A database uniqueness constraint protects the data at the actual storage boundary.

The application can still check first to provide a friendly message, but the database constraint remains important.

## CHECK

`CHECK` restricts a column to values that satisfy an expression.

For service duration:

~~~sql
duration_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL
    CHECK (duration_minutes > 0)
~~~

This prevents nonsensical values such as zero or negative duration.

For booking status:

~~~sql
status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'confirmed', 'cancelled'))
~~~

Now the database knows that these are the only valid statuses.

The application should still understand the same business rules, but the database prevents invalid states from being persisted.

## DEFAULT

A `DEFAULT` supplies a value when an INSERT does not provide one.

For example:

~~~sql
status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
~~~

This allows:

~~~sql
INSERT INTO bookings (
    customer_id,
    service_id,
    starts_at
)
VALUES (1, 2, '2026-10-10T10:00:00');
~~~

The database automatically stores `pending` as the status.

Defaults are particularly useful for predictable initial states such as a newly created booking, task or account.

## Why constraints belong in the database

It is tempting to think that validation belongs entirely in Java.

But the database has a different responsibility: **protect the integrity of the stored data regardless of which application writes it.**

For example:

~~~text
React validation
       ↓
Spring validation
       ↓
Service rules
       ↓
Database constraints
~~~

Each layer protects a different boundary.

The frontend improves user experience. The backend validates requests. The service enforces application rules. The database protects persistent data.

Some rules may exist at several levels because each layer can be bypassed independently.

## Foreign keys

A **foreign key** establishes a relationship between tables and lets the database enforce referential integrity.

Our booking table contains:

~~~sql
customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES customers(id)
~~~

You cannot insert a booking for customer ID 999 if customer 999 does not exist.

This prevents orphaned references.

Similarly:

~~~sql
service_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES services(id)
~~~

ensures that a booking refers to an existing service.

## ON DELETE behaviour

What should happen when a referenced row is deleted?

~~~terms
[{"term": "ON DELETE RESTRICT", "def": "Refuse to delete a parent that still has children (the safe default)."}, {"term": "ON DELETE CASCADE", "def": "Delete the children too — good for owned data like order items."}, {"term": "ON DELETE SET NULL", "def": "Keep the child, clear the link — e.g. a ticket whose assignee left."}]
~~~

SQL lets you define this with `ON DELETE` behaviour.

Three important choices are `RESTRICT`, `CASCADE` and `SET NULL`.

### RESTRICT

`RESTRICT` prevents the parent row from being deleted while dependent rows exist.

Conceptually:

~~~text
customer
   ↓
bookings

DELETE customer
      ↓
rejected because bookings exist
~~~

This is useful when deleting the parent while retaining the child records would not make sense and you want the application to deal with the dependencies explicitly.

### CASCADE

`CASCADE` deletes dependent rows automatically when the referenced row is deleted.

~~~sql
customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES customers(id)
    ON DELETE CASCADE
~~~

For the booking application, this means deleting a customer also deletes their bookings.

This can be appropriate when the child records have no meaningful existence without the parent.

Be careful: cascading deletes can remove many rows from one operation.

### SET NULL

`SET NULL` changes the foreign key to `NULL` when the parent is deleted.

~~~sql
customer_id INTEGER
    REFERENCES customers(id)
    ON DELETE SET NULL
~~~

The column must be nullable because the database needs somewhere to put `NULL`.

This can make sense when the child record should remain but its relationship to the deleted parent should disappear.

For example, you might keep historical records while allowing the original user account to be deleted.

Choose the behaviour based on the meaning of the data, not simply because one option is convenient.

## Naming conventions

In this course, we will use **snake_case** for database identifiers and plural table names.

Examples:

~~~text
customers
services
bookings
customer_id
duration_minutes
starts_at
~~~

This gives us a consistent convention across the schema.

Java classes will use Java naming conventions instead:

~~~text
CustomerEntity
BookingService
startsAt
customerId
~~~

The database and Java layers do not need identical naming conventions. Each ecosystem has its own conventions.

## Normalisation in plain English

**Normalisation** is a set of principles for organising relational data so that facts are stored in sensible places and unnecessary duplication is reduced.

You do not need to memorise every normal form to understand the useful idea.

Avoid repeated groups.

Bad design:

~~~text
customer_id
service_1
service_2
service_3
~~~

A customer can have any number of bookings, so repeated columns are the wrong model.

Instead, store bookings as separate rows:

~~~text
customer_id | service_id
------------+-----------
1           | 2
1           | 3
1           | 5
~~~

Also avoid duplicating the same fact unnecessarily.

Suppose the service duration is 60 minutes. Do not normally copy `60` into every booking while also storing it in the service table.

Store the service duration in `services`:

~~~text
services
id | name | duration_minutes
2  | Cut  | 60
~~~

Then the booking references service 2.

This gives one authoritative place for the service's standard duration.

## When denormalisation is useful

**Denormalisation** means intentionally duplicating or restructuring data to improve a particular use case, often performance or reporting.

For example, an analytics table might store a precomputed daily booking count instead of calculating it from millions of booking rows every time.

That can be a valid engineering decision, but it creates another copy of a fact that must stay consistent.

For the task manager and booking application, start with a straightforward normalised schema. Optimise after you understand the actual performance problem.

## Designing the booking schema

Let's put the ideas together.

Customers:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
~~~

Services:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE services (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    duration_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL
        CHECK (duration_minutes > 0)
);
~~~

Bookings:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE bookings (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL
        REFERENCES customers(id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE,
    service_id INTEGER NOT NULL
        REFERENCES services(id),
    starts_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
        CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'confirmed', 'cancelled'))
);
~~~

In PostgreSQL, we would normally use generated identity columns and an appropriate timestamp type for `starts_at`, for example:

~~~sql
id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
~~~

and:

~~~sql
starts_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
~~~

The browser exercise uses SQLite-compatible types so you can practise the schema rules without needing a PostgreSQL server.

## Common mistakes

### Storing multiple values in one column

Avoid values such as `service_ids = '2,4,7'`. Relational relationships should normally be represented with rows and foreign keys or a join table.

### Forgetting foreign keys

An integer called `customer_id` is not automatically a relationship. The foreign key constraint is what lets the database enforce that the referenced customer exists.

### Using nullable columns everywhere

If a value is required for a valid record, make it `NOT NULL`. Otherwise every application query has to consider another possible missing state.

### Relying only on application checks for uniqueness

A Java `if` statement cannot replace a database `UNIQUE` constraint when multiple requests can arrive concurrently.

### Choosing CASCADE without thinking

Cascade deletion is powerful. Deleting one parent can remove many child records. Use it only when that deletion behaviour matches the meaning of the data.

### Mixing naming conventions

Pick a convention and use it consistently. In this course, database tables and columns use plural table names and snake_case.

### Denormalising before there is a problem

Duplicating data can improve some workloads, but it also creates consistency problems. Start with a clear normalised model and measure before introducing deliberate duplication.

## The design principle to remember

A schema is more than a collection of tables. It describes what your application considers valid data.

Our booking model says:

~~~text
Customer
   │
   │ one-to-many
   ▼
Booking
   ▲
   │ many-to-one
   │
Service
~~~

Primary keys give rows identity. Foreign keys connect related data. `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK` and `DEFAULT` protect valid states. `ON DELETE` defines what relationships mean when data is removed.

The next lesson moves this schema into Java. You will create JPA entities and map these database relationships into classes that Spring Data can persist for you.
takeaways: A relational schema models domain facts as tables and connects related data with foreign keys.
Primary keys provide stable row identity, while UNIQUE constraints protect values that must not be duplicated.
NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT and foreign key constraints make the database enforce important data-integrity rules.
ON DELETE behaviour should reflect the meaning of the relationship rather than being chosen for convenience.
Normalisation reduces repeated groups and duplicated facts; denormalisation can be useful later when a measured requirement justifies it.

quiz.question: Where should the foreign key normally be stored for a one-to-many relationship between customers and bookings?
options: In the customers table as booking_id
In the bookings table as customer_id
In a third table that is always required
Foreign keys cannot represent one-to-many relationships
quiz.explanation: The foreign key belongs on the many side. Each booking stores the customer_id of its customer.

quiz.question:
What does this constraint enforce?

email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
options: Email may be NULL and duplicates are allowed
Every email must be present and no two rows may use the same email
Every customer must have exactly two emails
Email values are automatically encrypted
quiz.explanation: NOT NULL requires a value, while UNIQUE prevents duplicate values.

quiz.question: What happens with ON DELETE CASCADE on bookings.customer_id when the referenced customer is deleted?
options: The database automatically deletes that customer's bookings
The customer deletion is always rejected
The customer_id values become NULL while keeping the bookings
The service records are deleted instead
quiz.explanation: CASCADE propagates the deletion to dependent rows referencing the deleted parent.

quiz.question: Why is this a better relational design than storing service IDs as '2,4,7' in one column?
options: A comma-separated string is always faster
It avoids the need for primary keys
Each relationship can be represented and constrained as relational data
It prevents services from being reused
quiz.explanation: Relational data should normally represent relationships with rows, foreign keys and, where appropriate, join tables rather than encoded lists inside text columns.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a CHECK constraint such as CHECK (duration_minutes > 0)?
options: It automatically creates an index
It prevents invalid values that do not satisfy the condition
It makes duration_minutes nullable
It converts minutes into seconds
quiz.explanation: A CHECK constraint requires the inserted or updated value to satisfy its condition.

exercise.title: Design the booking schema
exercise.task: Write the CREATE TABLE statements for a small booking database. Create customers with exactly these columns: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE. Create services with exactly these columns: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, duration_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (duration_minutes > 0). Create bookings with exactly these columns: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, service_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES services(id), starts_at TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'confirmed', 'cancelled')). The setup already enables foreign keys with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;. PostgreSQL would use GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for the generated IDs and a TIMESTAMP type for starts_at; this browser exercise uses SQLite-compatible syntax. The tests will insert valid data, check the default booking status, verify that duplicate emails, zero duration, unknown customers and invalid statuses are rejected, and verify that deleting a customer deletes that customer's bookings.
exercise.starter:
-- Create customers, services and bookings here.

-- PostgreSQL note: production would normally use
-- GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for generated IDs
-- and TIMESTAMP for starts_at.
exercise.hint: Create customers and services before bookings because bookings references both tables. Put NOT NULL and UNIQUE directly on the customer columns. Use CHECK for the positive duration and allowed status values. The customer foreign key must include ON DELETE CASCADE; service_id does not need a delete action for this exercise.

tests.name: It accepts valid customers and services
It applies pending as the default status
It rejects invalid data
It cascades customer deletion to bookings
It prevents missing required values
